statement: The dollar will buy fewer Japanese yen on December 31, 2026 than on November 23, 2026.
why: One dollar buys nearly 160 yen, even after Japan's government spent close to 100 billion dollars buying yen to prop it up. In a Reuters poll, 86 in 100 economists expect the Bank of Japan to raise its interest rate to 1.50% at its meeting on December 17-18, and its governor, Kazuo Ueda, says the bank should keep raising. A higher rate, a government ready to buy yen again and a nervous stock market all tend to make the yen stronger. We are wrong if one dollar buys more yen at year end than on November 23, for example because the Bank of Japan does not raise its rate, or because a US rate rise makes the dollar more attractive.

statement: Bitcoin will be cheaper on December 4, 2026 than on November 23, 2026.
why: Bitcoin has fallen six weeks in a row and dipped below 62,000 dollars. Investors keep pulling money out of US bitcoin funds, and an expected US interest rate rise plus falling stock prices make people avoid risky bets. We expect the slide to go on for two more weeks. We are wrong if bitcoin costs more on December 4 than on November 23, for example because the steep fall tempts bargain hunters, or money starts flowing back into the bitcoin funds.

statement: Brent crude oil will be cheaper on December 31, 2026 than on November 23, 2026.
why: The price of Brent oil fell 4 in 100 last week, as tankers sailed through the Strait of Hormuz in about the same numbers as before the war. In October a barrel cost more than 116 dollars. The Middle East is pumping more oil, and falling stock prices hint that people and businesses will use less. We are wrong if a barrel costs more at year end than on November 23, for example because new attacks in the Iran war stop the tankers again, or OPEC+, the group of big oil producers, decides to pump less at its meeting on November 29.

statement: The interest the US government pays to borrow money for 5 years will be higher on December 11, 2026 than at the November 23, 2026 close.
why: Traders see the Fed's rate rise on December 9 as nearly certain. The Fed's rate now sits between 3.75 and 4 dollars a year per 100 dollars borrowed. One Fed governor said a bigger step than usual should be considered. Five-year borrowing costs track the Fed's expected path closely. With stocks recovering, the Fed has less reason to hold back. We are wrong if the 5-year rate is lower on December 11, for example because the inflation report out this Wednesday comes in soft or the Fed hints this is its last rise.

statement: Arabica coffee will be cheaper on March 31, 2027 than on November 23, 2026, when it closed near 267 cents a pound.
why: Brazil, the biggest grower, expects its arabica harvest to rise by about a third this year. Its coffee exports are surging, and coffee waiting for grading at exchange warehouses reached an eight-month high. We expect more supply to keep pulling prices down into spring. Coffee stored in exchange warehouses is near a 27-year low, and El Niño, a warm Pacific weather pattern, could bring dry weather to Brazil. Either could push prices up. We are wrong if arabica is above 267 cents a pound on March 31, 2027.

statement: Gold will be cheaper on December 4, 2026 than at its November 25, 2026 close, when it traded near 3,500 dollars an ounce.
why: Gold has lost about 10 in 100 of its value this month and slipped below 3,500 dollars an ounce this week, even while stocks fell. Today's hot inflation report all but settles a Fed rate increase in December. Higher rates make gold less attractive, because gold pays no interest. We expect the slide to continue for another week. We are wrong if gold is above today's close on December 4, for example if fear in markets brings buyers back to gold.
